title: Debt and cash flow
desc: Why profit isn’t cash, and what debt does to a company in a bad year

cards.added: Feedback for options the board doesn’t show written for the Academy
cards.title: Profit, but less cash?
cards.situation: Acme reports a $10M profit this year. Yet its bank balance fell by $5M. How can both be true?

options.feedback: Both can be right. A sale counts as profit when it’s made, but the cash arrives only when the customer pays.

options.text: Customers haven’t paid yet: profit isn’t cash
options.feedback: Profit counts the sale. Cash waits for the payment.

options.text: Profit and cash are always equal
options.feedback: They often aren’t. Profit counts a sale when it’s made; the cash arrives only when the customer pays.

cards.work: Acme booked $40M of sales but collected only $25M. The rest is still owed by customers.

cards.title: Cash pays the bills
cards.text: **[[cash-flow|Cash flow]]** is the money that really came in, minus what really went out. Wages, suppliers and loan interest are paid in cash, not in profit.

blocks.tip: A company can show a profit and still run out of cash.

cards.added: Tap notes written for the Academy (the working for each year)
cards.title: Debt in a bad year
cards.text: Two firms run the same business. One has no debt. The other pays $8M interest every year.

visual.title: Profit after interest
visual.label: Good year: $20M with no debt, $12M with big debt. Bad year: $6M and −$2M

groups.label: Good year
groups.note: No debt keeps $20M. Big debt: $20M − $8M interest = $12M.

groups.label: Bad year
groups.note: No debt keeps $6M. Big debt: $6M − $8M interest = −$2M, a loss.

cards.foot: Business earnings fell from $20M to $6M. Interest stayed at $8M, so the indebted firm made a loss.

cards.title: Profit that never turns into cash
cards.text: Profit rising every year while cash flow keeps going negative is a warning sign. Find out why: the money may never arrive.
cards.rule: check that profit turns into cash.

cards.added: Feedback for options the board doesn’t show written for the Academy
cards.title: A bad year with debt
cards.q: Northwind usually earns $15M before interest and pays $12M interest a year. This year it earns only $9M before interest. What’s left?

options.feedback: $3M profit is a normal year. Interest doesn’t shrink when earnings do.
Interest stays at $12M even in a bad year, and $9M of earnings can’t cover it.
Interest is set by the loan. It doesn’t shrink when earnings fall.
Interest is a cost, so you take it away from earnings, not add it.

cards.title: Same profit, different cash
cards.q: Both firms report a $10M profit. Acme turned it into $9M of cash. Northwind’s cash flow was −$2M. Which is on safer ground?

options.feedback: Same profit on paper, but Northwind’s cash went out, not in. Bills are paid in cash.

options.text: Acme: its profit arrived as cash
options.feedback: Bills are paid in cash, and Acme’s profit showed up in the bank as $9M. Northwind’s didn’t.

options.text: Same: profit is all that matters
options.feedback: Bills are paid in cash. Acme’s profit showed up in the bank. Northwind’s didn’t.
You can: compare how much of each profit arrived as cash. Acme +$9M, Northwind −$2M.

cards.headline: You can check cash and debt.
lines: Cash flow pays the bills. Profit can sit on paper.
Debt costs the same in good and bad years.
Profit that never becomes cash is a warning sign.
